title: Status and snapshot read unbounded direct-child files into memory
summary: `kcs status` and `kcs snapshot` call a shared working-tree builder that reads every included direct-child regular file wholly before any size limit. A lower-trust scope contributor can therefore drive local memory, I/O, and snapshot storage consumption through routine commands.

severity.rationale: A realistic lower-trust scope contributor can deterministically reach a victim resource sink through routine commands, so self-only suppression does not apply. The required matrix maps medium impact plus high likelihood to medium.
severity.changeConditions: Severity would rise if a bounded input can cause persistent or cross-scope service loss; it would fall once status and snapshot enforce a pre-read byte budget or stream hashing and storage without attacker-sized allocation.

confidence.rationale: V5+V10. Exact status and snapshot call graphs both terminate at an unconditional whole-file read. Repository tests cover small files only; no status/snapshot large/sparse-file bound was found.

taxonomy.category: resource consumption / local denial of service (CWE-400, CWE-770)

codeEvidence.label: Status reaches repository working-tree state
codeEvidence.explanation: The routine `status` command opens the selected scope and calls `repo.status()`, which reaches the shared working-tree builder.

codeEvidence.label: Builder reads each included file wholly
codeEvidence.explanation: After only direct-child, file-type, UTF-8-name, and exclusion checks, the builder calls `fs::read` and materializes the full attacker-sized file before hashing or storing it.

codeEvidence.label: Nearby size cap is later and adapter-specific
codeEvidence.explanation: `effective_max_input_bytes` is enforced only while selecting later adapter candidates, so it does not bound the earlier status or snapshot builder read.

rootCause.summary: The shared working-tree builder filters file type and name but then calls `fs::read` without a per-file or aggregate byte budget. The nearby `adapter.policy.max_input_bytes` check belongs to later adapter processing and does not protect status or snapshot.

remediation: Add a shared pre-read bound or streaming policy for status/snapshot; scan-hash and deferred-task reads are separate instances.

validation.summary: Exact status and snapshot call graphs both terminate at an unconditional whole-file read. Repository tests cover small files only; no status/snapshot large/sparse-file bound was found.
assertions: Exact status and snapshot call graphs both terminate at an unconditional whole-file read.
Repository tests cover small files only; no status/snapshot large/sparse-file bound was found.
counterevidence: Subdirectories, symlinks, and explicit exclusions are skipped.
Status does not persist bytes; snapshot holds the store lock.
The operator can remove the file and retry.
limitations: No large or sparse-file runtime measurement was retained; actual failure thresholds depend on host limits.

attackPath.summary: A lower-trust content contributor places a very large or sparse regular direct-child file in a scope the victim uses. The victim runs status or snapshot on that scope. The working-tree builder accepts the file through the type, name, and exclusion filters and calls fs::read before applying any byte ceiling. The victim process allocates and reads attacker-sized bytes; snapshot can additionally copy them into the archive, causing command failure or substantial local resource pressure.

reachability.summary: not public; reachable through local CLI processing of an adopted or shared scope
reachability.attacker: KCS runs as the victim OS user with that user's filesystem and memory limits; the attacker needs no KCS or OS-administrator identity
reachability.entrypoint: A lower-trust content contributor places a very large or sparse regular direct-child file in a scope the victim uses.
reachability.preconditions: plausible: control one included direct-child file and wait for the operator to run status or snapshot; sparse files can make the logical-size amplification inexpensive
reachability.outcome: runtime memory and I/O; snapshot also affects archive disk usage

impact.why: A realistic lower-trust scope contributor can deterministically reach a victim resource sink through routine commands, so self-only suppression does not apply. The required matrix maps medium impact plus high likelihood to medium.

likelihood.why: The selected scope is shared, supplied, or otherwise writable by a lower-trust content contributor. The hostile file is a direct regular child and is not explicitly excluded. The victim invokes a routine status or snapshot command.

counterevidence: The later effective_max_input_bytes control applies only to adapter processing and does not protect status or snapshot.
The command is recoverable after removing the file and does not create a confidentiality or authorization bypass.
limitations: No large or sparse-file runtime measurement was retained; actual failure thresholds depend on host limits.

remediationTests: Place a direct-child file just above the configured core limit and assert status and snapshot reject it before allocation or use bounded streaming.
Use a bounded sparse-file regression to confirm logical size cannot trigger unbounded materialization or dense snapshot expansion.
preventiveControls: Add a shared pre-read bound or streaming policy for status/snapshot; scan-hash and deferred-task reads are separate instances.
